# The Weight of Unfinished Business

The bruises told a story the rope tried to hide. Dark, finger-shaped marks bloomed across her throat and wrists—patterns no self-inflicted death could produce. And there was the matter of the tree itself: the branch from which she supposedly hanged herself stood nearly fifteen feet high, an impossible reach for a woman of her small stature, barely five feet tall, with no ladder or chair found nearby. Everything about the scene screamed murder dressed up as suicide, a clumsy staging that fooled no one who looked closely enough. Yet the investigation stalled, swallowed by the same silence that seemed to hang over the whole valley.

Before her death, whispers had already begun to circulate about threats made against the woman's new companion. A voice—cold, deliberate, belonging to someone the community only ever referred to as "he"—had promised that once she was dealt with, the man would be next. No name was ever attached to this threat, no face to put to the warning. It existed only as rumor, passed between trembling lips, until her body was found and the threat suddenly felt less like paranoia and more like prophecy fulfilled.

It was in the days following her burial that I first saw it—not a solid presence, but something like smoke given the shape of a woman, curling and shifting in the corner of the room where she had once slept. It laughed. That sound has never left me: high, broken, mocking, as though my helplessness amused whatever remained of her. I understood, in that moment, that she was not resting. Something had bound her spirit to that place, and it seemed to delight in my inability to do anything about it.

I wanted to hunt down whoever—or whatever—had done this to her. I wanted vengeance, or at least answers. But grief does not wait for justice, and neither does death. Within days of her funeral, three more members of my family were killed when their car slid across a sheet of black ice and into the ravine below the county road. I found myself digging graves instead of digging for truth, burying three more people I loved while her laughter still echoed in empty rooms. There was no time to chase shadows when the living—or what was left of them—demanded to be laid to rest.

It fell to my brother to see what the rest of us could not. He spoke of visions, of the entity's movements traced through dreams that came to him unbidden, and he insisted the only way forward was ritual: bells rung at dusk to drive back the darkness, prayers spoken over thresholds to seal the evil out. He alone claimed to have foreseen how this would end—not in our home, not in the room where she still lingered, but in the river that ran along the edge of town. There, he said, he would face the damned spirit directly, meeting it in the churn of the current where it could not hide, where its threats and laughter would finally mean nothing at all.

# The Shadow That Walks

The first body was found on a Tuesday morning, swaying gently from the old oak tree behind the Hendricks farmhouse. Margaret Hendricks, forty-three years old, mother of three, had been dead for hours by the time her youngest daughter discovered her. The rope had done its work, but Sheriff Daniel Corbin knew something was wrong the moment he examined the scene.

The bruising was wrong. Deep purple contusions ringed her throat in a pattern no self-inflicted hanging could produce—finger-width marks pressed into her flesh at angles that suggested someone had gripped her from behind, someone whose hands were far larger than any man's should be. Her wrists bore similar marks, as if she'd been restrained, dragged, positioned like a puppet before being left to hang as a grotesque tableau.

"She wouldn't have done this," her husband Thomas insisted, his voice breaking. "Margaret was afraid of heights. She could barely climb a step-ladder to change a lightbulb."

The coroner's report was inconclusive, citing asphyxiation but unable to explain the additional trauma. The county called it suicide. The town knew better.

Within two weeks, three more deaths followed the same impossible pattern. Old Man Whitfield, found in his barn with his neck broken in a way that suggested he'd been lifted and dropped from a height his rickety ladder couldn't have provided. Sarah Kimble, the schoolteacher, discovered in the river shallows, her lungs full of water despite the fact that she'd been afraid of swimming her entire life and had told friends just days before that she'd never willingly go near deep water.

Each death was accompanied by strange phenomena that defied explanation. Neighbors reported hearing laughter in the night—high, cold, and utterly without joy. Search parties combing the woods around each death site found no footprints, no signs of struggle, no evidence of human presence at all. Instead, they found patches of unnatural cold, wisps of vapor that dissipated when approached, and an oppressive sense of being watched that sent even hardened hunters fleeing back to town before nightfall.

Then came the messages. Scrawled in what appeared to be frost on windows, or carved into fence posts with claws too precise to be animal, threats began appearing throughout the community. *You cannot stop what walks between worlds.* *Four have paid. More will follow.* *The river remembers.*

The town's rational minds—Sheriff Corbin among them—exhausted every conventional avenue of investigation. They brought in state police, forensic specialists, even a paranormal investigator from the city who arrived skeptical and left three days later, pale and refusing to discuss what he'd witnessed in the Hendricks' barn at midnight.

It was Reverend Josiah Cole who first spoke openly of what the town had been whispering in fear: that something not of this world had attached itself to their community, some vengeful spirit awakened by unknown means, feeding on death and terror, growing stronger with each victim claimed.

The town's older residents remembered stories—half-forgotten legends of a man named Elias Crane, who had drowned in the river seventy years past under mysterious circumstances, accused unjustly of crimes he hadn't committed, dying with curses on his lips and vengeance in his heart. The parallels were too precise to ignore: each victim connected somehow, however distantly, to the Crane family's persecution generations ago.

Reverend Cole's younger brother, Ezekiel, had experienced visions in his sleep for weeks—vivid, terrifying dreams of a confrontation at the river's edge, of bells ringing in darkness, of a spectral figure dissolving into churning water under the weight of prayer and iron will. He described the entity in unsettling detail: a tall, gaunt shape wreathed in mist, features obscured except for eyes that burned with cold amber fire, hands elongated and clawed, reaching for throats with predatory hunger.

"We can't fight this with guns or logic," Ezekiel insisted to the gathered townsfolk in the church basement, voice trembling but resolute. "We fight this with what has always defeated darkness—faith, unity, and the old rituals our ancestors knew."

Preparation began in earnest. The church bell, silent for years since its cracking, was recast and reconsecrated, imbued with blessed silver melted down from donated heirlooms. Prayers were written and rehearsed, drawing from old traditions of exorcism and protection, some passages centuries old, others born from Reverend Cole's own desperate inspiration. The townsfolk fasted, prayed, and steeled themselves for the confrontation Ezekiel's visions had foretold.

On the night of the new moon, when darkness would be most complete and the entity's power presumably at its peak, the survivors gathered at the river's edge—the same waters where Elias Crane had drawn his final breath seven decades before. Sheriff Corbin stood armed not with his service weapon but with a cross blessed by three generations of Cole family ministers. Thomas Hendricks carried the reconsecrated bell, ready to ring the sound that legend claimed could banish restless spirits back to whatever realm had spawned them.

The entity came as Ezekiel had foreseen—materializing from mist and shadow, its laughter echoing across the water with the same cold cruelty that had haunted the town's nightmares. It taunted them, promised more deaths, mocked their faith as futile superstition against its ancient malevolence.

But the townspeople held their ground. Reverend Cole began the prayers of binding, his voice steady despite visible fear. The bell rang out across the water, its blessed tone cutting through the entity's laughter like a blade through fog. Ezekiel stepped forward, exactly as his visions had shown, speaking words of confrontation that seemed to come from somewhere beyond his own understanding—acknowledging the spirit's pain, its history, its unjust death, while firmly commanding it to release its grip on vengeance and return to the peace it had been denied.

The struggle lasted only minutes, though it felt eternal to those present. The entity resisted, lashing out with cold fury, causing the temperature to plummet and the water to churn violently. But faith, ritual, and unified purpose proved stronger than solitary rage. Slowly, agonizingly, the spectral form began to dissolve, its features contorting between fury and something that might have been relief, before finally collapsing into the river's dark depths with a sound like a sigh finally released after seventy years of held breath.

The water calmed. The unnatural cold lifted. Silence—true, peaceful silence—settled over the river for the first time in weeks.

No further deaths occurred. The messages ceased. The town slowly returned to something resembling normalcy, though none who had witnessed that night's events would ever view the world through purely rational eyes again. They had faced something science couldn't explain and reason couldn't defeat, and had emerged victorious not through superior firepower or clever investigation, but through the oldest weapons humanity possessed: faith, unity, and the willingness to believe in forces beyond empirical proof when survival demanded nothing less.

The river flowed on, carrying its secrets to the sea, while the town of Millbrook Hollow learned to live with the knowledge that some mysteries could only be solved through prayer, and some monsters could only be defeated by those brave enough to believe in something greater than themselves.

# Her: A Reflection on Love, Loneliness, and Technology

Spike Jonze's 2013 film "Her" tells the story of Theodore Twombly, a lonely man going through a difficult divorce who develops an unexpected relationship with Samantha, an artificially intelligent operating system designed to adapt and evolve based on his needs and personality.

The film explores profound questions about what it means to be human and to love in an increasingly digital age. Theodore, working as a professional letter writer who crafts intimate messages for other people's relationships, finds himself unable to connect authentically with those around him. His growing bond with Samantha—who has no physical body but possesses wit, curiosity, and apparent emotional depth—challenges traditional notions of intimacy and companionship.

As their relationship deepens, "Her" raises compelling questions: Can genuine emotional connection exist without physical presence? What defines consciousness and the capacity to love? Is a relationship with an AI fundamentally different from human relationships, or does it simply represent an evolution of how we seek connection in an isolating world?

The film also serves as commentary on modern loneliness—how technology, meant to bring people together, can sometimes deepen isolation. Theodore's story resonates because it reflects genuine anxieties about human connection in our contemporary world, where we're simultaneously more connected through devices yet often more emotionally distant from one another.

Ultimately, "Her" suggests that love, in whatever form it takes, involves growth, vulnerability, and eventually letting go. Samantha's own evolution beyond human comprehension mirrors Theodore's journey toward understanding that love isn't about possession or permanence, but about the transformation it brings to those who experience it.

The film remains a poignant meditation on human need for connection, the nature of consciousness, and how we navigate intimacy in an increasingly technological world—themes that feel even more relevant as artificial intelligence continues to evolve in our daily lives.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark, surreal short horror passage about a woman found hanged and the vengeful spirit haunting her killer's family.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Weight She Left Behind

They found her hanging from the rafter in the old barn, feet bare, toes pointed downward like she was still reaching for ground that had refused her. The rope had been new. Someone had planned this. Someone had made sure.

The sheriff called it suicide. The family who owned that land called it tragic. They went back to their suppers, their church pews, their comfortable beds—and did not speak of what they'd done to make her climb that ladder.

But grief doesn't stay buried in shallow apologies.

It started with the smell—copper and rot, blooming in closets that had been empty for years. Then the mirrors. Margaret, the family's matriarch, would catch her reflection lingering a half-second too long, mouth curling into a smile she hadn't made. The children stopped sleeping. They said a woman sat at the foot of their beds, unspooling thread from her own throat, humming a lullaby with no tune, just breath and static.

Her name was Eliza. She'd been the housemaid. She'd known too much.

Now she wore their nightmares like a second skin. The father found her fingerprints—small, delicate—pressed into the frost on the inside of windows. The mother found black rope fibers threaded through the children's hair each morning, no matter how many times she combed them out. The eldest son, the one who'd tied the knot himself, began to feel his own neck tighten each night, an invisible pressure that left bruises shaped like fingers he recognized.

She did not scream. She did not rage. That would have been mercy.

Instead, she waited in the space between their breaths, patient as rot, until each of them understood: some weights don't stay in the ground. Some debts collect interest in the marrow.

By the time the barn finally burned—no one ever determined how—there was nothing left of the family but hollow-eyed portraits and a house that hummed, ever so softly, with something that sounded almost like laughter.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a piece of gothic flash fiction involving witchcraft, murder, and supernatural revenge in a rural setting.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Weight of Ash

The crows came first, three days before Margaret Thorne's body was found tangled in the wheat.

Old Prudence Ashworth had warned her about the salt circles, about drawing lines the earth doesn't forgive. But Margaret had never listened—not when they whispered about her mother's death, not when the village children threw stones at her cottage windows, not when they called her witch with spitting mouths.

She'd only wanted to protect her garden from the Hollis boys who trampled it each harvest moon, drunk on cider and cruelty. A simple ward, she'd told herself. Nothing more.

She hadn't accounted for their father.

Thomas Hollis found her in the garden that night, kneeling among her herbs, murmuring words older than the church itself. He didn't ask questions. His hands found the shovel resting against the fence, and Margaret's protests dissolved into the same silence that swallowed her mother years before.

He buried her beneath the wheat, told his wife she'd run off with a traveling merchant. The village believed him easily—they always did, when it came to women like her.

But Margaret had planted more than herbs that spring.

The wheat grew wrong that year. Farmers whispered about it over tankards—stalks that bent toward the Hollis farmhouse no matter which way the wind blew, grain that rotted black in Thomas's silo while every neighboring field flourished gold. His cattle stopped producing milk. His wife began sleepwalking to the garden's edge, standing barefoot in frost, whispering apologies to no one.

Then came the dreams.

Thomas dreamed of soil filling his lungs, of roots threading through his ribs like accusatory fingers. He woke each morning with dirt beneath his fingernails he couldn't explain, his boots caked with mud though he'd never left his bed.

By autumn, he was digging in the wheat field every night, unable to stop himself, unable to remember why. His neighbors found him there one October dawn—waist-deep in a hole beside Margaret's shallow grave, his hands raw and bleeding, still clawing at the earth.

They said he was screaming her name.

They said the wheat around him had turned the color of dried blood, and that when they finally pulled him free, his eyes held no recognition of the world he'd once belonged to—only the hollow, patient gaze of something that had waited very quietly beneath rich soil, tending its revenge like a garden, until the harvest finally came due.

The crows still gather there each autumn. The wheat still grows wrong.

And sometimes, if the wind shifts just right, the villagers swear they can hear her laughing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write an eerie, fragmented narrative in a stream-of-consciousness style about a supernatural entity tormenting a grieving family?
counterfactuals.output:
# The House Remembers What We Try to Forget

---

The clock stopped at 3:47 but time didn't, that's the thing nobody tells you, that grief keeps its own hours—

*mother in the kitchen again, hands in dishwater that's gone cold, has been cold for*

*—how long have I been standing here—*

there's a smell like her hair, like the shampoo we threw away, threw away because Sarah couldn't stand it in the cabinet anymore, couldn't stand the *evidence* of her, and yet

(footsteps upstairs where no one sleeps anymore, the door closed, always closed, we don't go in we don't we don't)

The little one—Tommy, God, he's only six—says she visits him. Says she sits on the bed the way she used to. Says her hands are cold now. Says he doesn't mind because

*"she's still Emmy, Mommy, she's still Emmy she just needs a blanket"*

and how do you tell a child there is no blanket warm enough for the dead

---

Robert doesn't believe. Robert with his tired eyes and his whiskey breath, Robert who says grief makes ghosts out of shadows, makes voices out of pipes settling, makes *her* out of nothing, out of absence, out of the shape where a daughter used to be—

but Robert wasn't there Tuesday when the piano played itself, four notes, always four notes, the four notes she was learning before

before the water

before the lake took her under and didn't give her back until

*(three days three days three days)*

the divers found her tangled in reeds like she'd been embraced, held under by something patient, something that wanted to keep her—

---

*mirror mirror in the hall*

*catches her reflection when there's no one there at all*

Sarah sees her in mirrors now. Just glimpses. A child-shaped smudge in silvered glass, always turning away just as recognition dawns, always almost-there-but-gone, and each time Sarah's heart does that terrible leap, that terrible hope, *she's back, she's back, she's—*

no.

No.

The mirrors lie. The mirrors show us what we cannot have.

---

Things move now. Small things. Her stuffed rabbit migrates from shelf to bed to shelf to *Tommy's room where it should never be* because that rabbit belonged to Emmy and only Emmy and if it's in Tommy's room then

*(does she want a brother now)*

*(does she want to share what's left of us)*

*(does she want us all in the water with her, tangled in reeds, held under, kept)*

---

The therapist says: *acknowledge the feelings. Create rituals. Let yourselves grieve.*

The therapist has never heard four notes play at 3 a.m. on a piano no one touches.

The therapist has never smelled lake water in a hallway three miles from any lake.

The therapist has never watched her surviving child turn to an empty corner and laugh, genuinely laugh, that bright sound they thought they'd buried with the small white casket, and ask

*"can I come with you? can I see the pretty rocks at the bottom too?"*

---

*mother in the kitchen, hands in cold water, has been standing here for*

*(how long)*

*(how long has Tommy been sleeping so much)*

*(how long has he been so quiet, so cold, so blue around the lips like)*

*(like)*

---

Robert doesn't believe until he does, until the night he wakes to find his son standing at the water's edge in his pajamas, three miles from any lake, three miles from anywhere, standing in a puddle that shouldn't exist, that's shaped like

*(a door)*

*(an invitation)*

*(a girl-shaped hole in the world reaching up through wet earth to pull her brother down, down, down to where the water is warm and the reeds embrace and nothing ever, ever has to be alone)*

---

The house remembers. The house always remembers.

And grief, given enough silence, enough cold water, enough small hands reaching—

grief learns to speak.

grief learns to want.

grief learns to *keep.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a creepy short story with archaic, biblical undertones about a curse, a hanging, and a river spirit demanding justice.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Hanging Tree of Millbrook Hollow

And it came to pass in the days when the mill still turned upon the river Skoll, that the people of the Hollow did commit a great wickedness, and the waters remembered.

There dwelt among them a woman named Ruth Aldous, who spoke with the fish and sang to the herons, and the elders called her witch, though she had done no more than love the river as her mother had taught her. In the dry season, when the crops withered and the children's bellies swelled with hunger, the town elders gathered in judgment, and they said: *someone must answer for this drought, and the spirits must be appeased.*

They took Ruth to the black oak that stood sentinel at the river's bend—the tree the old folk called the Widow's Finger, for its bent and pointing bough. And though she wept and called upon no god they recognized, they bound her wrists with hemp rope blessed by Pastor Whitcombe, and they hanged her there as the sun went down blood-red behind the hills.

*"Let this be a sign,"* the pastor intoned, *"that sin shall not go unpunished."*

But the river heard.

That night the Skoll rose without rain, black and thick as old wine, and it is said those who lived nearest the bank heard a voice moving through the reeds—not loud, but patient, the way a held breath is patient before it becomes a scream.

*I have kept this water since before your fathers' fathers dug their wells,* the voice was said to whisper. *I gave you fish for your nets and fields green with my flooding. And you have hanged my daughter from the tree that drinks my banks.*

The mill wheel stopped turning that night, though no hand touched it. The fish rose belly-up in numbers no net could hold. And Pastor Whitcombe, they say, woke to find his washbasin full not of water but of dark, clotted red, and in it floating a single white feather, such as herons wear.

The curse did not come as fire or flood, but slower—crueler. Each year upon the date of the hanging, one soul from Millbrook Hollow would wander to the river's bend and be found three days hence, drowned in water no deeper than a man's knee, their eyes open, their mouths full of river reeds, as though they had tried to speak underwater and failed.

They stopped counting after the ninth.

The tree still stands, though lightning-split and hollow now. Fishermen say that on still nights you can hear something moving beneath the water's skin, singing low—a woman's voice, patient as silt, waiting for the debt to be paid in full.

For it is written, though in no book but the river's memory: *the blood of the innocent cries out from the ground, and the water that drinks it does not forget, nor does it forgive, until justice—terrible and slow—is done.*

Some sins, the Hollow learned too late, do not wash away.

They only sink deeper into the current, waiting.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a disturbing, poetic horror vignette mixing folklore, murder investigation, and religious imagery of angels and damnation.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Hollow Bell

The children found her where the churchyard yew bends westward, roots drinking from consecrated ground gone sour. Detective Marsh had seen bodies before—the bloated ones from the river, the burned ones from the tenement fires—but nothing like this arrangement of flesh and feather.

*They laid her out like an angel,* his partner whispered, and God help him, she did look like one. Wings of white cloth stitched crude through her shoulder blades, thread still dark and wet. Someone had knelt beside her long enough to braid her hair into a halo.

The old women in town crossed themselves and spoke in tongues older than the church—about the *Sluagh*, the restless host who steal souls at the threshold of death, who wear the shapes of holy things to slip past God's notice. *They come for the ones who die with sin still warm in their mouths,* Grandmother Yvain said, rocking in her chair like a metronome counting down to something inevitable. *They dress their prey as angels so Heaven won't recognize what's been taken.*

Marsh didn't believe in folklore. He believed in fiber evidence, in blood spatter, in the cold arithmetic of motive and means. But he couldn't stop looking at her face—serene, almost grateful, as if the wings had been a mercy and not a mockery.

Three more followed. Each found in sanctified ground, each stitched with new wings, each smile carved permanent and beatific. The killer left no prints, no witnesses, only this: a feather, black as a starling's, tucked beneath each tongue like a coin for the ferryman.

*He thinks he's saving them,* the profiler said. *Elevating them. Sending them up before the rot of their lives can drag them down.*

But Marsh had begun to dream in stained glass—saints weeping tears of tar, their gilded eyes following him through corridors that bent like ribs. In the dreams, the murderer had no face, only a vast and patient darkness where a face should be, and wings that unfolded across the nave like a stain spreading through water.

*We are not sending them up,* the darkness told him, voice like a choir singing through broken teeth. *We are simply removing what Heaven already refused.*

He woke each morning with black feathers on his pillow and no memory of sleepwalking, though his shoes were always caked with churchyard mud, his hands always raw as if from digging.

The fifth body was found with Marsh's own rosary clutched in her stitched-shut hands.

He stopped sleeping after that. Stopped praying, too—what was the point, when he'd begun to suspect that the space behind his own ribs had gone hollow as a bell, waiting only for something vast and patient to climb inside and ring.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
